Starting by applying the triangle inequality to the second expression in equation~\eqref{eq:constr}, and then applying Cauchy--Schwarz to $-q$ to obtain a second inequality, we learn:
    $$
\begin{aligned}
2N|a|
&\leq 2(n+1)+|q(y,\delta)| \\
&\leq 2(n+1)
   + \sqrt{|q(y,y)|}\sqrt{2(n+1)} \\
&\leq 2(n+1)
   + \sqrt{2(n+1)}
     \bigl(|a| \sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2(n+1)}\bigr) \\
&= 4(n+1)
   + \sqrt{2(n+1)}(|a| \sqrt{2}) .
\end{aligned}
$$
    where line 3 followed by rearranging the first expression of equation~\eqref{eq:constr}. Rearranging the final inequality for $|a|$, we learn that for $N$ large $|a|<1/2$, and is thus zero. In particular $y=\delta'$ lies in $H^\perp$.

    Since we know $a=0$, the second formula of equation \eqref{eq:constr} ensures that $q(y,\delta) = -2(n+1)$. Thus using condition (2) of Definition~\ref{defn:K2nH} twice we find that $$q(y-\delta,y-\delta) = q(y,y) -2q(y,\delta) +q(\delta,\delta) = 0.$$ But $y,\delta\in H^\perp$ where $-q$ is positive definite, so this is only possible if $(\delta' =) y=\delta$.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- definition-52: body_md -->
\label{defn:genKummerLocus}
    Fix once and for all an integer $N>N_0$ with $N_0$ as in Proposition \ref{prop:TangentSpaceANDUniquePointwise}. Further assume that $N_0$ is sufficiently large to ensure that $NH-\delta$ is ample for any $A$ an abelian surface. We write $\mathcal{K}_{2n}^\circ$ for the \textit{generalised Kummer locus}: the connected component in $\operatorname{NL}(N)$ whose closed points are of the form $(\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(A),NH-\delta)$ where $A$ is a principally polarised abelian surface.
<!-- end definition-52 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:resolveComment}
    The locus of Definition~\ref{defn:genKummerLocus} is a connected component in $\operatorname{NL}(N)$.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
We will show that it is both open and specialisation closed. Specialisation closed because Proposition \ref{prop:HodgeTheoryRecall} forces the Hodge structure to degenerate whenever the abelian variety degenerates. It is open because, as follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:TangentSpaceANDUniquePointwise}(1), the map from $\mathcal{A}_2$ induces an isomorphism on tangent spaces at each point.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- definition-53: body_md -->
Let $\mathsf{Aut}(A)$ be the group of automorphisms of $A$ as polarised abelian variety. Let $\mathsf{Aut}(\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(A))$ be the group of automorphisms of $\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(A)$ as a sheaf on the category of logarithmic schemes.
<!-- end definition-53 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:AMGpAnyField}
    For any integer $n\geq 2$ the morphism $\varphi_{2n}$ is an injection of groups.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
The preimage of the identity in $A$ under the summation map $A^{(n+1)}\rightarrow A$ is denoted $K_{(2n)}$. The Hilbert--Chow morphism $A^{[n+1]}\rightarrow A^{(n+1)}$ restricts to define a map $\operatorname{HC}\colon \operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(A)\rightarrow K_{(2n)}$, and this map is an isomorphism on the dense open of both source and target where the support consists of $n+1$ points. 
    
    One can construct a morphism $$\varphi_{(2n)}\colon T_{n+1}\rtimes \mathsf{Aut}(A)\rightarrow \mathsf{Aut}(\operatorname{K}_{(2n)})$$ similarly to the construction of $\varphi_{2n}$. The images of an element of $T_{n+1}\rtimes \mathsf{Aut}(A)$ under $\varphi_{2n}$ and $\varphi_{(2n)}$ agree on the common open subset defined by $\operatorname{HC}$. Since an automorphism is determined by its restriction to a scheme-theoretically dense open by \cite[Tag~\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01RH}{01RH}]{stacks}, it will suffice to show that $\varphi_{(2n)}$ is injective. 
    
    A point of $K_{(2n)}$ is the data of $n+1$ sections of $A/\Delta_0$ which sum to the identity. We write these supports as an unordered tuple $(p_0,...,p_n)$ of points on $A$ and reiterate that $\sum_i p_i$ is trivial in the group law on $A$. 
    
    
    There is a map which is injective on closed points from $A$ to $\operatorname{K}_{(2n)}$ sending $a$ to $(a,...,a, -na)$. Restriction defines a map $$\operatorname{Im}(\varphi_{2n})\rightarrow T_{n+1}\rtimes\mathsf{Aut}(A)$$ whose image is precisely the automorphisms of $A$ which send the identity to a point of the $(n+1)$-torsion. This map is a splitting of $\varphi_{(2n)}$ and thus $\varphi_{(2n)}$ is injective.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- remark-20: body_md -->
\label{rem:ClassicalCase}
    For $A$ an abelian surface over $\mathbb{C}$ the morphism $\varphi$ is known to be an isomorphism to the collection of automorphisms which preserve the Hilbert--Chow exceptional divisor, see \cite{BOISSIERE2011553}. We expect the same statement remains true in the logarithmic category.
<!-- end remark-20 -->
<!-- definition-54: body_md -->
Recall $\mathcal{Y}_2(n+1)\rightarrow \mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$ is the universal logarithmic abelian surface (Section~\ref{sec:ModulilogAVLevelStr}) over the moduli space of logarithmic abelian surfaces with $(n+1)$-level structure. We write $$\pi_{n+1}\colon Y_2(n+1):=\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(\mathcal{Y}_2(n+1)/\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)) \rightarrow \mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$$
    for the associated logarithmic Kummer variety.
<!-- end definition-54 -->
<!-- definition-55: body_md -->
Define a finite group,
$$
G_{n+1}=(\mathbb{Z}/(n{+}1)\mathbb{Z})^{4}\rtimes 
\mathsf{Sp}_{4}(\mathbb{Z}/(n{+}1)\mathbb{Z}),
$$ where $\mathsf{Sp}_{4}(\mathbb{Z}/(n{+}1)\mathbb{Z})$ acts upon $(\mathbb{Z}/(n{+}1)\mathbb{Z})^{4}$ via the standard representation.
<!-- end definition-55 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:GroupActionGerbe}
    Let $n\geq 2$ be an integer. There is an action of $G_{n+1}$ upon ${Y}_2(n+1)$ satisfying the following hypotheses.
    \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin = *]
        \item The morphism $\pi_{n+1}$ is $G_{n+1}$-equivariant, and thus descends to a morphism of quotient stacks
        $$\mathcal{U}_{2n}\coloneqq[{Y}_2(n+1)/G_{n+1}] \rightarrow \mathcal{K}_{2n}\coloneqq [\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)/G_{n+1}].$$
        \item Let $p$ be a standard logarithmic geometric point of $\mathcal{K}_{2n}$ and let $A_p/p$ be the abelian surface specified by any point of its preimage in $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$. The gerbe structure at $p$ in $\mathcal{K}_{2n}$ is the group $(\mathbb{Z}/(n+1)\mathbb{Z})^4\rtimes \operatorname{Aut}(A_p)$ and the action on $\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(A_p)$ is induced by the morphism $\varphi_{2n}$ described after Definition~\ref{sec:AutLogKummer}.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
The universal family over $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$ is, by definition of level structure, equipped with an identification of finite \'etale $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$ group schemes, $$h\colon (\mathbb{Z}/(n+1)\mathbb{Z})^4_{\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}_2[(n+1)],$$ where $\mathcal{Y}_2[(n+1)]$ is the $(n+1)$-torsion of $\mathcal{Y}_2(n+1)$. The group $(\mathbb{Z}/(n{+}1)\mathbb{Z})^{4}$ acts upon $\mathcal{Y}_2(n+1)$ by sending $y$ to translation through $h(y)$. The group $\mathsf{Sp}_{4}(\mathbb{Z}/(n{+}1)\mathbb{Z})$ acts as follows: an element $g$ specifies a new framing $g\circ h$ and thus, through the universal property of $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$, an automorphism of $\mathcal{Y}_2(n+1)$. By construction $\mathsf{Sp}_{4}(\mathbb{Z}/(n{+}1)\mathbb{Z})$ the map $\pi_{n+1}$ is $G_{n+1}$ equivariant.

    Every automorphism of a logarithmic abelian surface which fixes the $(n+1)$-torsion is the identity \cite[Lemma 5.1]{KajiwaraKatoNakayamaPartVII}, and thus $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$ has trivial stabiliser groups. It follows that the gerbe structure at a point $p$ in $\mathcal{K}_{2n}$ associated to abelian surface $A\rightarrow p$ is the stabiliser of any point in the preimage of $p$ within $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$. In particular, the stabiliser group is the subgroup $K$ of $G_{n+1}$ which fixes the abelian variety $A$. The group $K$ certainly contains the normal subgroup $(\mathbb{Z}/(n+1)\mathbb{Z})^4$ of $G_{n+1}$ and is thus determined by its image in $G_{n+1}/(\mathbb{Z}/(n+1)\mathbb{Z})^4$. But this image is exactly the stabiliser of $A$ in the moduli of logarithmic abelian surfaces without level structure, and thus coincides with $\text{Aut}(A)$.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- definition-56: body_md -->
The stack quotient $\mathcal{K}_{2n}\coloneqq [\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)/G_{n+1}]$ is called the \textit{logarithmic generalised Kummer locus}, and the morphism $\mathcal{U}_{2n}\rightarrow \mathcal{K}_{2n}$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:GroupActionGerbe}(1) is the \textit{universal logarithmic generalised Kummer variety}.
<!-- end definition-56 -->
<!-- definition-57: body_md -->
\label{defn:polarisation}
    Given a family of principally polarised logarithmic abelian surfaces $(A\rightarrow S,H)$, we define a polarisation upon $A^{n+1}$ by tensoring the principal polarisation pulled back along each projection to $A$. This polarisation descends to a polarisation $\mathcal{L}$ on the stack quotient (and thus also on the coarse space of) $A^{n+1}/\text{Sym}(n+1)$. The Hilbert--Chow map of the relative Hilbert scheme, $$A^{[n+1]}\rightarrow A^{n+1}/\text{Sym}(n+1)$$
    is a resolution of singularities with exceptional divisor $E$. We define a polarisation upon $A^{[n+1]}$ through the formula $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes N}\left(- \frac{1}{2}E\right)$ and note this restricts to a polarisation on $\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(A)$.
<!-- end definition-57 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{prop:NLlocus}
    The family $$\pi^{\operatorname{str}}\colon \mathcal{U}_{2n}^{\operatorname{str}} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}_{2n}^{\operatorname{str}},$$ equipped with the polarisation of Definition~\ref{defn:polarisation}, induces an isomorphism of conventional DM stacks $$k \colon \mathcal{K}_{2n}^{\operatorname{str}}\rightarrow \mathcal{K}_{2n}^\circ.$$
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
The morphism $\pi^{\operatorname{str}}$ together with the polarisation of Definition \ref{defn:polarisation} define a morphism from $\mathcal{K}_{2n}^{\operatorname{str}}$ to the moduli of polarised IHS varieties of generalised Kummer type. By construction the image lies within $\mathcal{K}_{2n}^\circ$ and thus we have a morphism $$k\colon \mathcal{K}_{2n}^{\operatorname{str}} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}_{2n}^\circ.$$ 
    We will now show that $k$ is an isomorphism of DM stacks.
    
    \textbf{Step I: k is \'etale.} We claim that $k$ induces an isomorphism of tangent spaces at each point. Let $p$ be any point of $\mathcal{K}_{2n}^{\operatorname{str}}$ and choose any point $x$ in the preimage of $p$ in $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$. Write $A$ for the abelian surface associated to $x$, and set $H\in H^2(A,\mathbb{Z})$ its polarisation class. Since $G_{n+1}$ is \'etale, the tangent space at $p$ is canonically identified with the tangent space at $x$. The period map identifies the tangent space of $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$ at $x$ with $H^\perp$ in $H^2(A,\mathbb{C})$. 
    On the level of period maps $k$ is the inclusion of $H^2(A,\mathbb{C})$ into $H^2(\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(A),\mathbb{C})$ described in Proposition~\ref{prop:HodgeTheoryRecall}. Under this inclusion, $H^\perp\cap H^{1,1}(A,\mathbb{C})$ in $H^2(A,\mathbb{C})$ is mapped isomorphically to $\langle H,\delta \rangle^\perp\cap H^{1,1}(\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(A),\mathbb{C})$ in $H^2(\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(A),\mathbb{C})$. But by Proposition~\ref{prop:TangentSpaceANDUniquePointwise}(1) (and Lemma~\ref{lem:resolveComment}) $\langle H,\delta \rangle^\perp$ in $H^2(\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(A),\mathbb{C})$ is the tangent space of $\mathcal{K}_{2n}^\circ$ at $k(p)$, and the identification of tangent spaces is proved.

    Any morphism of smooth complex DM stacks which induces an isomorphism on tangent spaces at every point has locally equidimensional fibres and so miracle flatness applies. Thus $k$ is flat. The isomorphism of tangent spaces further forces $k$ unramified. Flat and unramified maps are \'etale.

\textbf{Step II: k induces a bijection on $\mathbb{C}$-points.} Surjectivity is by construction: it remains to prove injectivity. By Proposition~\ref{prop:TangentSpaceANDUniquePointwise} the polarised variety $(X,L)$ specified by a geometric point of $\mathcal{K}_{2n}^\circ$ determines the class $\delta$ which is half the class of the exceptional divisor of the Hilbert--Chow map. The orthogonal complement of $\delta$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb{Z})$ under $q$ is thus determined, and by Proposition \ref{prop:HodgeTheoryRecall} we obtain $H^2(A,\mathbb{Z})$. But knowing $H^2(A,\mathbb{Z})$ determines $A$ up to dualising by the main theorem of \cite{Shioda1978ThePM}. Since $A$ admits a principal polarisation it is self dual, and $A$ is determined. It remains to show that the polarisation on $A$ is determined.

The polarisation class add $\delta$ divided by $N$ determines a class $H$ in a polarised Hodge structure isomorphic to $H^2(A,\mathbb{Z})$ with square $2$. Note that $H$ is ample on $A$ and thus effective. We need to show that this polarisation class is well defined independent of the choice of isomorphism between this abstract polarised Hodge structure $\delta^\perp$ and $H^2(A,\mathbb{Z})$. We will adopt notation of \cite{Shioda1978ThePM}, and in particular this allows us to discuss the determinant of a morphism between two lattices isomorphic to $H^2(A,\mathbb{Z})$. If there are two choices of isomorphism between $\delta^\perp$ and $H^2(A,\mathbb{Z})$ this gives an automorphism of $H^2(A,\mathbb{Z})$ as a polarised Hodge structure. If this automorphism of $H^2(A,\mathbb{Z})$ has determinant one then by \cite[Lemma 1]{Shioda1978ThePM} either it will send an ample class to minus an ample class, or it is induced by an isomorphism on $H^1(A,\mathbb{Z})$ and thus an automorphism of $A$. Since at most one of $H$ or $-H$ is effective, $H$ is determined. If instead our automorphism of $H^2(A,\mathbb{Z})$ has determinant $-1$ then we can compose with the morphism $H^2(A,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H^2(A^\vee,\mathbb{Z})$ of \cite[Lemma 3]{Shioda1978ThePM} which the same reference shows has determinant $-1$. We have thus reduced to the determinant $1$ case.

\textbf{Step III: $k$ is representable by algebraic spaces.} For $N$ large, and $A$ a (conventional) abelian variety, all polarised automorphisms of $\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(A)$ preserve the Hilbert--Chow exceptional. Thus by Remark~\ref{rem:ClassicalCase}, the morphism on stabiliser groups induced by $k$ at all $\mathbb{C}$ points is an isomorphism. The morphism of inertia stacks $\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{K}_{2n}^{\operatorname{str}}}\rightarrow \mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{K}_{2n}^\circ}\times_{\mathcal{K}_{2n}^\circ} \mathcal{K}_{2n}^{\operatorname{str}}$ induced by $k$ is an isomorphism by \cite[Tag~\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0DU9}{0DU9}]{stacks}. 
Invoking \cite[Tag~\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/04Z6}{04Z6}]{stacks}, the relative inertia stack is isomorphic to $\mathcal{K}_{2n}^{\operatorname{str}}$. 
It now follows from \cite[Tag~\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/04YY}{04YY}]{stacks} ((3) implies (1)) that $k$ is representable by algebraic spaces. 

\textbf{Step IV: Conclusion.} Since $\mathcal{K}_{2n}^\circ$ is a Deligne--Mumford stack of finite type, \'etale locally it is of the form $[V/G]$ for $G$ a finite group, and by representability of $k$ this morphism is \'etale locally a map $$[\widetilde{V}/G]\rightarrow [V/G],$$ induced by an \'etale map of algebraic spaces $k'\colon \widetilde{V}\rightarrow V$. By orbit-stabiliser theorem, bijectivity of $k$ on geometric points implies bijectivity of $k'$ on geometric points. Thus $k'$ is an \'etale map of algebraic spaces of finite type over $\mathbb{C}$ which induces a bijection on geometric points. Such spaces are Jacobson, and thus $k'$ is an \'etale monomorphism so an open immersion which surjects on closed (and thus all by Jacobson property) points. We deduce that $k'$ is an isomorphism, but being an isomorphism is \'etale local on the target so our proof is complete.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:squarefromMainThm}
    There are compatible actions of $G_{n+1}$ on $\mathpzc{A}_2(n+1)$ and $\mathpzc{Y}_2(n+1)$, such that the commutative square of Theorem~\ref{thm:commuting square} descends to a diagram of stack quotients,
      $$\begin{tikzcd}
\mathcal{U}_{2n} \arrow[r, "\widetilde{\varpi}_\mathcal{U}"] \arrow[d, "\pi"'] 
& a^\ast [\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(\mathpzc{Y}_2(n+1))/G_{n+1}]=\colon a^\ast\mathpzc{U}_{2n} \arrow[d, "a^\ast \pi^{\mathsf{trop}}"] \\
 \mathcal{K}_{2n} \arrow[r, "\varpi_\mathcal{K}"] 
& a^\ast  [\mathpzc{A}_2(n+1)/G_{n+1}] =\colon  a^\ast \mathpzc{K}_{2n}
\end{tikzcd}.$$  
in which the horizontal maps are strict.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Note that $G_{n+1}$ acts upon the objects of Definition~\ref{defn:TropAVLevel} exactly as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:GroupActionGerbe}. The same argument establishes a $G_{n+1}$ equivariant commutative square, which descends to a diagram of quotient stacks. Since strictness can be checked strict \'etale locally, this property descends to our quotient square.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:GettingModels} We establish the following.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin = *]
    \item For any diagram of stacks upon the tropical site, 
    $$
    \begin{tikzcd} 
    \mathpzc{U}_{2n}^\Lambda \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"\pi"]
  & \mathpzc{U}_{2n} \arrow[d] \\
\mathpzc K_{2n}^\Lambda \arrow[r]
  & \mathpzc{K}_{2n}.
\end{tikzcd}$$
    where the horizontal maps are tropical alterations, and $\pi$ is a saturated morphism of cone stacks, the morphism
    $$\mathcal{U}_{2n}^\Lambda = \mathcal{U}_{2n}\times_{a^\ast \mathpzc{U}_{2n}}a^\ast \mathpzc{U}^\Lambda_{2n}\rightarrow \mathcal{K}_{2n}^\Lambda = \mathcal{K}_{2n}\times_{a^\ast \mathpzc{K}_{2n}} a^\ast \mathpzc{K}^\Lambda_{2n}$$
    is a vertical, saturated, and logarithmically smooth morphism of DM stacks with logarithmic structure.
    
    \item The open immersion $\mathcal{K}_{2n}^\circ \hookrightarrow \mathcal{K}_{2n}^\Lambda$ is a toroidal compactification.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Note (1) can be checked \'etale locally on $\mathcal{K}_{2n}^\Lambda$, which is \'etale locally atomic. Thus (1) follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:ProperLogSmooth}. Claim (2) can also be checked \'etale locally, and $\mathcal{K}_{2n}$ admits an \'etale cover by $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$ by construction, so the result follows from \cite[Theorem~1.8]{KajiwaraKatoNakayamaPartVII}.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{prop:KnBehaved} We record the following properties of the logarithmic generalised Kummer locus.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The morphism $\operatorname{KumSh}(\mathcal{A}_2)\rightarrow \operatorname{KumSh}(\mathcal{K}_{2n})$ induces an isomorphism at the level of coarse moduli spaces.
    \item The stack $\mathcal{K}_{2n}$ is a proper logarithmic DM stack.
    \item The stack $\mathcal{U}_{2n}$ is a proper logarithmic DM stack.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
For (1) observe that kummer log \'etale locally every principally polarised logarithmic abelian variety admits a level (n+1) structure \cite[Proposition 18.1(3)]{KajiwaraKatoNakayamaPartIV}. Thus the fibre over a test scheme $S$ in the category fibred in groupoids $\operatorname{KumSh}(\mathcal{A}_2)$ is the groupoid which can be presented with objects the maps from $S$ to $\operatorname{KumSh}(\mathcal{A}_2(n+1))$ and morphisms induced by the action of $\operatorname{Sp}_4(\mathbb{Z}/(n+1)\mathbb{Z})$. The fibre over $S$ in the category fibred in groupoids $\operatorname{KumSh}(\mathcal{K}_{2n})$ admits a presentation with the same objects and morphisms induced by $G_{n+1}$. It suffices to show that the setoids associated to the groupoids named above coincide. Equivalently, two maps from $S$ to $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$ are identified by $G_{n+1}$ if and only if they are identified by $\operatorname{Sp}_4(\mathbb{Z}/(n+1)\mathbb{Z})$. This is true because the action of $\mathbb{Z}/(n+1)\mathbb{Z}$ on $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$ is trivial.

    For (2) we first check that $\mathcal{K}_{2n}$ is a logarithmic DM stack. Indeed $\mathcal{K}_{2n}$ is defined as the global quotient stack of $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$ by the action of a finite \'etale group scheme. Composing with the projection, every logarithmic \'etale cover of $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$ thus induces a logarithmic \'etale cover of $\mathcal{K}_{2n}$. 
    
    Properness is invariant under logarithmic modifications and Kummer root stacks, and is thus invariant under all logarithmic alterations. Indeed for passing to a root stack this is clear, and invariance under logarithmic modification holds because the valuative criterion of \cite[Theorem~2.2.5.2]{MolchoWise} tests only against valuative test schemes, and whenever $S$ is valuative the $S$-valued points of a logarithmic space $X$ are invariant under logarithmic modifications of $X$. It thus suffices to check that $\mathcal{K}_{2n}$ admits a proper logarithmic alteration. We will show that $\mathcal{K}_{2n}^\Lambda$ is proper. Indeed, it is the global quotient stack of $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)\times_{\mathcal{K}_{2n}} \mathcal{K}_{2n}^\Lambda$ by a finite group, and $\mathcal{A}_2(n+1)$ is proper by \cite[Theorem~1.6]{KajiwaraKatoNakayamaPartVII}.

    An \'etale cover of $\mathcal{K}_{2n}$ pulls back along the universal morphism to an \'etale cover of $\mathcal{U}_{2n}$. Claim (3) follows by combining claim (2) with Proposition~\ref{prop:ProperLogSmooth}.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
\label{ex:AbSurface1}
    Fix positive integers $\alpha, \beta$. Let $S=\mathbb{A}^2_{u,v}\backslash V((u^\alpha-1)(v^\beta-1))$ be affine space over $\mathbb{C}$ less $\alpha + \beta$ lines, with toric logarithmic structure and coordinates $u$ and $v$. 
    We write $S^\circ$ for the complement of $V(uv)$ inside $S$. 
    Consider the morphism, $$W = \mathbb{P}^2_{x_1,y_1,z_1}\times \mathbb{P}^2_{x_2,y_2,z_2}\times S\rightarrow S$$ and write $W^\circ= W\times_S S^\circ$. 
    Let $\hat{A}$ be the surface over $S$ whose ideal in $\mathcal{O}_W$ is given by: $$\left(y_1^2z_1 -x_1 (x_1-z_1)(x_1-u^\alpha z_1),y_2^2 z_2 - x_2 (x_2 - z_2)(x_2 - v^\beta z_2)\right),$$ and write $A^\circ$ for the abelian scheme $\hat{A}\times_S S^\circ$ over $S^\circ$.
    Thus $A^\circ$ is the product of two degenerating elliptic curves. Note that $\hat{A}\rightarrow S$ is logarithmically smooth, and thus $$A = \operatorname{Pic}^0_S(\operatorname{Pic}^0_S(\hat{A}))\rightarrow S$$ is a (and thus the) family of logarithmic abelian varieties over $S$ whose restriction over $S^\circ$ is $A^\circ$.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
\label{ex:TropAV1}
    We record the tropicalisation associated to Example \ref{ex:AbSurface1}, whose notation we continue. The tropical abelian variety is $\mathpzc{A}(\varphi)$, where $\varphi$ is the morphism $$\mathbb{Z}^2\rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}^2,\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{N}^2,\mathbb{Z})\cong \mathbb{Z}^2), \quad (s,t) \mapsto \left((a,b)\mapsto (2a \alpha s, 2b \beta t )\right).$$
    The total space of $\mathpzc{A}(\varphi)$ is of real dimension four (being a tropical abelian surface over $\sigma$ which has dimension two), and a depiction is far beyond the author's artistic skill. Instead we depict two instructive slices. First, choose a ray $(p=\text{log}(u),q=\text{log}(v))$ in $\mathbb{N}^2$ and pull our family of tropical abelian varieties back to this ray. Below centre we assume $p,q\ne 0$, and the associated integral affine manifold is of real dimension two. Right and left we assume precisely one of these parameters is zero (if both are zero then no degeneration has occurred and the tropicalisation is a point). Algebro-geometrically left and right are type~II degenerations of abelian surfaces, while centre is type~III.
    \begin{figure}

<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:IAmRep}
    The functor of points of $A_\alpha$ on $\textbf{RPC}_\rho$ represents $\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(\mathpzc{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
A map from a test cone $\tau$ to $\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(\mathpzc{A})$ is $n+1$ unordered sections $(s_1,...,s_{n+1})$ of $$\mathpzc{A}_\tau:=\mathpzc{A}\times_\rho \tau\rightarrow \tau$$ which do not meet over the interior of $\tau$ unless they coincide. If the image of (the interior of and thus the whole of) $\tau$ is $0$ in $\rho$ then the only map from $\tau$ to both $\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(\mathpzc{A})$ and $A_\alpha$ is the zero map. 
    
    If the interior of $\tau$ is not mapped to $0$ in $\rho$ then we proceed as follows. 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           
                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              
                                                    
                    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             
    Each $s_i$ is an equivalence class of elements in $\mathsf{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathsf{Hom}(\tau,\mathbb{Z}))= \mathsf{Hom}(\tau,\mathbb{Z}).$ 
    The equivalence relation identifies two elements where their difference lies in the image of $\varphi$. Choose lifts $\hat{s}_1,...\hat{s}_{n+1}$ of the sections $s_i$ to $\mathsf{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathsf{Hom}(\tau,\mathbb{Z}))$ satisfying the following properties: 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Considered functions on $\tau$, for any $i,j$ we have $|\hat{s}_{i}-\hat{s}_j|\leq|\varphi(1)|$ at each interior point of $\tau$.
        \item In the group law of $\mathsf{Hom}(\tau,\mathbb{Z})$ there is an equality $\sum_i\hat{s}_i = 0$.
    \end{enumerate} 
    Fix a point $t$ in the interior of $\tau$. The first equality can be ensured at $t$ by repeatedly subtracting $\varphi(1)$ from the largest representative. Once true at $t$ it is true for all points in the interior of $\tau$ because the original sections $s_i$ were assumed not to meet over the interior of $|\tau|$. Once condition (1) is achieved, condition (2) can be made to occur at the same time: the sum of lifts satisfying the first condition can be written $m\varphi$ for some $m$ because the $s_i$ sum to zero in the group law of $\mathpzc{A}$. If $m>0$ then choose $j$ such that $\hat{s}_j(t)$ is maximal, and replace $\hat{s}_j$ by $\hat{s}_j-\varphi(1)$. This decreases $m$ by $1$: repeat until $m=0$. If $m<0$ then add $m\varphi(1)$ to each $\hat{s}_i$ and we are in the case $m>0$. In the sequel we consider $\hat{s}_i$, and thus $s_i$ to be ordered by their value on $t$, and note this ordering is independent of the choice of $t$. Relabelling, we assume the ordering is $s_1\leq s_2\leq ...\leq s_{n+1}$
    
    We now define elements of $\operatorname{Hom}(\tau,\mathbb{N})$, $$g_i = \hat{s}_{i+1}-\hat{s}_i\text{ for }1\leq i \leq n \text{ and } g_{n+1} = \varphi(1) + \hat{s}_1-\hat{s}_{n+1}.$$ The $g_i$ together specify a map $\tau \rightarrow \mathbb{N}^{n+1}$. Combining with the map from $\tau$ to $\rho$ specifies a map $$\tau\rightarrow \mathbb{N}^{n+2}.$$
    Note that summing the $g_i$ gives $\varphi(1)$, which ensures that the image satisfies the first equality in the definition of $A_\alpha$. Also we can write $$\hat{s}_i = \hat{s}_1 + \sum_{j<i} g_j \text{ for }i<n+1$$ and thus the summing to zero condition ensures that $$(n+1)\hat{s}_1 = \sum_i (i-n-1)g_i.$$ Taken modulo $n+1$ this implies the second equality. Together the last two displayed equations demonstrate that $\hat{s}_i$, and thus the map from $\tau$ to $\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(\mathpzc{A})$, can be recovered from the map from $\tau$ to $A$. We have thus constructed our bijection. Every step was functorial in $\tau$, and thus the result is proved.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin = *]
        \item The map $\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(\mathpzc{A})\rightarrow \rho $ is represented by an integral morphism of cone complexes whose link is, as a topological space, an n-simplex. The vertices of the polyhedral structure on this simplex are precisely vertices of the simplex. 
        \item The map $\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(A)\rightarrow \Delta$ is a vertical, proper, and integral morphism of DM stacks with logarithmic structure. 
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Note (2) follows from (1) by Theorem~\ref{thm:GettingModels}. 
    For (1) we know that $\rho$ is represented by a cone complex (it is a ray).
    By Lemma \ref{lem:IAmRep}, $\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(\mathpzc{A})$ is a cone complex. Integrality is the same as asking that the associated morphism of toric varieties is flat. Since all toric varieties are Cohen--Macaulay, and the toric variety $\mathbb{A}^1$ associated to $\rho$ is regular, this flatness property is immediate from equidimensional fibres by miracle flatness.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
\label{ex:LP}
    Let $\alpha = 8$. We now specialise to the $n=2$ (fourfold) case, where a degeneration was already constructed in \cite{halle2026degenerationsgeneralizedkummervarieties}. 
    The preimage of $1$ in $\rho$ inside the monoid $A_8$ consists of 15 points\footnote{Note not every ray contributes a point - we have not saturated and so this is not necessary.} on the link as depicted by red crosses in Figure \ref{fig:hhz}.

    The reader is entitled to choose a logarithmic alteration $\mathpzc{A}_{\operatorname{LP}}\rightarrow \mathpzc{A}$ which introduces rays which pass through every integral point in the preimage of $1$ in $\mathpzc{A}\rightarrow \rho$. The resulting logarithmic alteration $A_{\operatorname{LP}} = A\times_\mathpzc{A}\mathpzc{A}_{\operatorname{LP}}\rightarrow A$ is semistable over $\Delta$ and its central fibre is a cycle of $\alpha=8$ ruled surfaces. 

    The inclusion of the universal tropical subscheme into $\mathpzc{A}^{[3]}\times \mathpzc{A}$ together with the projection map define morphisms: $$\mathpzc{Z}_3\rightarrow \mathpzc{A}^{[3]}\times \mathpzc{A} \rightarrow \mathpzc{A}$$
    Taking the common refinement of the cone complex structure pulled back from $\mathpzc{A}_{\operatorname{LP}}\rightarrow \mathpzc{A}$ with the locally closed stratification of $\mathpzc{A}^{[3]}\times \mathpzc{A}$ induced by $\mathpzc{Z}_3$ defines a subdivision of piecewise linear spaces  $\Sigma'\rightarrow \mathpzc{A}^{[3]}\times \mathpzc{A}$. Pushing forward the induced locally closed stratification of $\mathpzc{A}^{[3]}\times \mathpzc{A}$ induced by $\Sigma'$ to $\mathpzc{A}^{[3]}$ specifies a tropical alteration $\Sigma\rightarrow \mathpzc{A}^{[3]}$, and thus a subdivision of $\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(\mathpzc{A})$. The link of this subdivision is depicted in Figure \ref{fig:hhz}.
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- example-8: body_md -->
\label{ex:HHZ}
    The dual intersection complex of the Type~II degenerations constructed in \cite{halle2026degenerationsgeneralizedkummervarieties} can naturally be considered a refinement of the subdivision described in Example \ref{ex:LP}. This refinement is shown as light grey with lines dashed in Figure \ref{fig:hhz}.

    Rational points of the link in Figure \ref{fig:hhz} biject with unordered tuples of three points $k_1,k_2,k_3\in \mathbb{Q}/8\mathbb{Z}$ which sum to $0$ mod $8$. Each point $k_i$ may be written in the form $$2a_i + \epsilon_i d_i \text{ where }a_i\in\{0,1,2,3\}, \quad \epsilon_i\in\{\pm 1\}, \text{ and } d_i \in [0,1].$$ The grey lines subdivide the simplex such that on the interior of each face the order of $d_i$ is constant.
<!-- end example-8 -->
<!-- definition-58: body_md -->
\label{defn:Aug}
    Fix points $u,v\in \mathbb{Z}^2$ which generate a lattice $\Lambda$. Given a configuration of points $(p_1,...,p_k)$ upon $\mathbb{R}^2/\Lambda$, we define the \textit{augmented subdivision} of $\mathbb{R}^2/\Lambda$ as follows.
    \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin = *]
        \item First define a subdivision $\Sigma^\text{pre}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2/\Lambda$ which is a polyhedral complex\footnote{So the cone over this structure is a subdivision of the integral affine manifold $\mathpzc{A}$ by a cone complex.} as follows. First define a $\Lambda$ equivariant subdivision of $\mathbb{R}^2$ by placing a vertex at each point of $\Lambda$, and an edge between any two vertices $n_1,n_2$ such that $n_1-n_2 \in \{\pm u,\pm v\}$. The resulting subdivision of tropical abelian varieties specifies a logarithmic alteration of the logarithmic abelian variety $A\times_S\mathbb{A}^1$.
        \item Next for each element $p_1,...,p_k$ of our configuration we impose a vertex at $p_i+\lambda$ for all $\lambda \in \Lambda$, and further pass to the minimal subdivision such that the straight line between $p_i +\lambda_1$ and $p_i + \lambda_2$ is a union of cones whenever $\lambda_1-\lambda_2$ is either a multiple of $u$ or $v$. 
        \item The above subdivision is $\Lambda$ equivariant and thus descends to the quotient.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-58 -->
<!-- definition-59: body_md -->
\label{defn:SquareSubdiv}
    The square subdivision of $\mathpzc{A}^{[n+1]}$ is obtained by pushing forward the cone complex structure on its universal family described in Definition~\ref{defn:Aug}. The square subdivision of $\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(\mathpzc{A})$ is the subdivision obtained by pulling back the square subdivision of $\mathpzc{A}^{[n+1]}$ along the tautological inclusion.
<!-- end definition-59 -->
<!-- remark-21: body_md -->
The procedure of Definition~\ref{defn:SquareSubdiv} defines the trivial polyhedral subdivision if performed upon the integral affine manifold associated to a type~II degeneration.
<!-- end remark-21 -->
<!-- example-9: body_md -->
In the $n=1$ case the resulting polyhedral subdivision of a sphere (and thus dual intersection complex) is obtained by connecting the red dots of the central sphere of Figure \ref{fig:TropGenKummerFibres} to form a square.
<!-- end example-9 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:tidyup}
    In the $n+1=s$ case, the square subdivision has $$n(n+1)+1 +\frac{n(n+1)(n^3+6n^2+3n+2)}{24}$$ vertices, and thus we have specified a type III degeneration whose special fibre this many components.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
Note that points in $\operatorname{Kum}_{2n}(\mathpzc{A})$ biject with tuples of $n+1$ points on $\mathbb{R}^2/\Lambda$ which sum to zero. We first characterise when a point in $\operatorname{Sym}^{n+1}(\mathbb{R}^2/\Lambda)$ gives rise to a vertex in the square subdivision. Let $(p_1,...,p_{n+1})\in \operatorname{Sym}^{n+1}(\mathbb{R}^2/\Lambda)$ and let $S_u$ (resp $S_v$) be the set of points $t$ in $[0,1)$ such that there exists some integer $i\in \{1,...,n+1\}$ and real number $t'$ such that $p_i$ can be represented by $tu + t'v$ (resp. $t'u + tv$) in $\mathbb{R}^2$. 
    
    We claim that if $(p_1,..,p_{n+1})$ is a vertex then both $S_u$ and $S_v$ contain at most one real number which is not $0$. Assume for contradiction that $S_u$ contains two non-zero real numbers $a,b$, and suppose that $n_a$ of the $p_j$ can be written $au + xv$ for some real $x$ and $n_b$ of the $p_j$ can be written $bu + xv$.  To reach a contradiction we will construct a path starting at $(p_1,...,p_{n+1})$ on which the combinatorial type is constant. This is done by changing points as follows:
    \begin{enumerate} 
        \item Whenever $p_j$ can be written $au + x_jv$ for some real number $x$, replace $p_j$ with $(a + \epsilon n_b)u + x_j v$. 
        \item Whenever $p_j$ can be written $bu + x_jv$ for some real number $x$, replace $p_j$ with $(b - \epsilon n_a)u + x_j v$.
    \end{enumerate}
    The condition that points sum to zero is preserved in the $u$ direction by construction, and in the $v$ direction because those coordinates were not changed. Varying $\epsilon \geq 0$ moves our point without changing its combinatorial type. Thus $(p_1,...,p_j)$ is not a vertex and we have a contradiction.

    Conversely, if $S_u$ and $S_v$ contain at most one non-zero point, then the sum zero condition means that $(p_1,...,p_j)$ cannot be deformed without changing its combinatorial type - it is a vertex.
    We now count cases.
    \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
        \item If $S_u= S_v = \{0\}$ then we know that $(p_1,...p_{n+1})$ is the origin - we have precisely one vertex.
        \item If $S_v = \{0\}$ but we are not in case 1, then suppose there are $w$ points of the form $au + xv$ with $a\ne 0$. We know that $wa=0$ mod $1$ and $wa\ne 0$, so there are $w-1$ possibilities for the value of $a$. Summing over all possible values of $w$ gives $$\sum_{w=2}^{n+1}(w-1)=\frac{(n+1)n}{2}$$ vertices.
        \item If $S_u = \{0\}$ but we are not in case (1), then as in case (2) we have ${n(n+1)}/{2}$ vertices.
        \item If neither $S_u$ nor $S_v$ is $\{0\}$ then we proceed as follows. The number of tuples $(p_1,..,p_{n+1})$ with $n_a\geq 1$ vertices with $u$ coordinate $a$, and $n_b\geq 1$ vertices with $v$ coodinate $b$ is the number of $2x2$ non-negative integer matrices whose second row sums to $n_a$, second column sums to $n_b$, and whose entries sum to ${n+1}$. Indeed, we are looking for ways to allocate ${n+1}$ vertices over the four possible positions $\{(a,0),(0,0), (0,b), (a,b)\}.$ There are $$1 + \operatorname{min}\{n_a,n_b,{n+1}-n_a,{n+1}-n_b\}$$ such matrices.\footnote{Four dimensions of 2x2 matrix, three linear relations gives one degree of freedom which is adding a multiple of $(1,-1;-1,1)$. The formula is then a direct computation.} Once again there are $(n_a-1)$ (resp. $(n_b-1)$) possible values of $a$ (resp. $b$). The total contribution is thus $$\sum_{n_a = 2}^{n+1}\sum_{n_b = 2}^{n+1} (1 + \operatorname{min}\{n_a,n_b,{n+1}-n_a,{n+1}-n_b\})(n_a-1) (n_b-1)
=
\frac{n(n+1)(n^3+6n^2+3n+2)}{24}.
$$
    \end{enumerate}
    The final result is obtained by summing the contribution from each of our four cases.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
